analysis.one_liner: Lets workers use state insurance and wage laws against benefit plan denials.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote, after the Labor and Health and Human Services Departments submitted unfavorable comments.
analysis.plain_summary: A 1974 federal law, ERISA, blocks most state lawsuits over job-based benefits, including claims that an insurance company handled a benefits claim in bad faith. This bill would have carved three exceptions: state laws that let people sue insurers for unfair claim practices, state prevailing-wage laws, and state apprenticeship and training rules. It also directed the Labor Department to study how ERISA's preemption of state laws affects workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers and their families covered by job-based health, disability, and life plans. Today, when an insurer denies or delays a benefits claim unfairly, ERISA generally blocks the worker from suing under state law, and the damages available under federal law are very limited [S2][S3]. The bill would have restored state-law remedies, letting workers recover under their state's insurance rules. It also would have protected state prevailing-wage laws and apprenticeship standards from being overridden by ERISA challenges [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers in employer health and benefit plans

how_it_helps.text: Amends ERISA so that state laws providing remedies against insurance companies for unfair practices in administering employee benefit plans or processing claims are not preempted [S2][S3].
Protects state prevailing-wage laws from ERISA preemption, so states can enforce wage standards on covered work without federal override [S2][S3].
Protects state laws setting standards for apprenticeship and other training programs, including rules making certified training an occupational qualification [S2][S3].
Directs the Secretary of Labor to study the effects of ERISA preemption of state laws relating to employee benefit plans and report recommendations to Congress [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Insurance companies, which would once again face state-court lawsuits and damages for unfairly denying or mishandling benefits claims, and employers and plan sponsors, who could face more litigation and state-by-state regulatory variation in how they run benefit plans [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers and employers sponsoring benefit plans

drawbacks.text: Repealing preemption in this area would expose insurers and employers to differing state-by-state standards, raising compliance costs and litigation risk for multi-state benefit plans, costs that can be passed back into premiums [S2][S3].
ERISA's uniform federal standard was adopted partly to let employers run one nationwide plan rather than 50 different state regimes; reopening state remedies works against that uniformity [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers with unfairly denied claims, the gain is real: under ERISA's preemption they generally cannot recover meaningful damages under state law, which the bill would have changed [S2][S3]. The cost is a more fragmented legal landscape for employers and insurers, which could push up benefit costs. The bill took a measured approach, carving out only three categories of state law and ordering a broader study of preemption's effects [S2][S3].

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which held a subcommittee hearing but never voted it out, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced April 9, 1991 by Senator Metzenbaum (for himself and Senator Kennedy) and read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources [S3][S5].
The Senate Labor Subcommittee held hearings on April 16, 1991, printed as S.Hrg. 102-231 [S5].
On September 29, 1992, the committee received executive comments from the Departments of Labor and Health and Human Services that were unfavorable to the bill [S5].
The committee never reported the bill, and no vote was ever taken in either chamber before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insurance companies and employers with benefit plans are better off, because ERISA's preemption of state-law claims over unfairly handled benefits was left fully intact. Workers whose claims are denied under employer plans remain limited to ERISA's narrow remedies.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers; workers' state-law claims stay blocked

for.name: Sen. Howard Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Labor and Human Resources Committee; his Labor Subcommittee held hearings on it in April 1991.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; original cosponsor

against.name: Departments of Labor and Health and Human Services
against.what_they_did: Submitted unfavorable executive comment on the bill to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee in September 1992.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Held a subcommittee hearing but never reported the bill to the Senate floor, letting it die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken. All sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats, while the unfavorable executive comments came from Republican administration agencies, but the bill died in a Democratic-controlled committee without a recorded position.

industries.note: The bill would have stripped away ERISA's shield that blocks state-court suits over unfair handling of employee benefit claims, exposing insurers to state bad-faith remedies and damages. Insurers' interest ran against workers seeking redress for denied claims.

industries.industry: Employers and plan sponsors of employee benefit plans
industries.note: Employers would have faced greater litigation exposure and state-by-state regulation of the plans they sponsor, since ERISA's uniform federal standard would no longer override the covered state laws.

State certification and registration standards for apprenticeship programs would have been insulated from ERISA challenges, tightening requirements for programs that fail to meet state minimums while stabilizing rules for compliant ones.
